strengths: Introduces a model-aware inference-time noise selection framework (ANSE) for video diffusion, using attention-based uncertainty instead of external noise priors.
Proposes BANSA and a Bernoulli-masked approximation that enables multiple stochastic attention samples from a single forward pass, plus a layer-selection strategy to reduce cost.
Evaluates on CogVideoX-2B and 5B with VBench, generating a large number of videos and providing ablations on acquisition function, K, M, temporal scope, and reversed selection.
Reports consistent improvements over random/vanilla in quality, semantic, and total scores with modest inference overhead (+8.7% and +13.8%).
Provides qualitative examples and discusses limitations, including failure cases where low BANSA does not guarantee perceptually strong generations.
weaknesses: Serious mathematical/sign inconsistency: Eq. (4) in the main paper defines BANSA with the opposite sign from the BALD-style implementation used in the appendix. Under Eq. (4), minimizing the score would select high disagreement/uncertainty, contradicting the paper's stated goal of selecting low-uncertainty noise; the appendix later flips the sign. This undermines the central technical formulation.

The Bayesian justification is weak: Bernoulli masking of attention logits is not posterior sampling over model parameters, and the BALD analogy is heuristic rather than a principled Bayesian treatment of attention uncertainty.

Evaluation lacks the most relevant baselines: FreeInit and FreqPrior are omitted, and there is no comparison to other noise optimization/selection methods or to a best-of-M random/oracle selection upper bound. The claim that prior methods are unsupported is not sufficient for a top-tier empirical paper.
Generalization claims are overstated: only CogVideoX-2B and CogVideoX-5B from the same model family are tested, not 'various text-to-video architectures' as claimed.

Performance gains are very small: total VBench score improves by only +0.63 for 2B and about +0.19–0.25 for 5B (with an arithmetic inconsistency in Table 1/text). No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported, so the improvements may be within evaluation noise.

Layer-selection details are inconsistent and potentially problematic: the main paper says correlation with full-layer BANSA scores, while the appendix says correlation with VBench quality scores, using prompts from VBench categories—raising concerns about tuning on evaluation data and unclear generality.

Computational comparisons to prior methods are not directly measured; the claimed ~64% reduction versus FreeInit/FreqPrior is extrapolated from a 3× sampling assumption rather than benchmarked. Memory overhead is also not measured despite claims of unchanged memory.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code link or released artifacts are evident, and key implementation details such as selected attention types/layers and exact score computation pipeline are not fully specified.
Ethical/societal impact is not discussed, despite the method directly improving text-to-video generation quality, which raises misuse concerns.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant problem: initial noise seeds strongly affect video diffusion outputs, and inference-time seed selection is a sensible direction.
The proposed pipeline is relatively lightweight and integrates into pretrained CogVideoX models without retraining or modifying the sampling process.
The empirical study is broad in terms of generated videos (4,730) and includes ablations over acquisition functions, ensemble size K, noise pool size M, and reversed scoring.
The qualitative examples and limitation section candidly acknowledge failure cases and the gap between attention uncertainty and perceptual quality.
weaknesses: Critical technical inconsistency: Eq. (4) defines BANSA as mean entropy minus entropy of the mean (negative mutual information), but Appendix B says the implementation uses the opposite BALD-style sign. Algorithm 1 selects argmin under Eq. (4), which would actually select the most disagreeing/uncertain attention maps, contradicting the central claim that low BANSA means confident and consistent attention. The proof of Proposition 1 also uses the BALD-style sign rather than the main definition.

The Bayesian framing is not justified. Bernoulli masking of attention logits before softmax is not posterior sampling over model parameters and does not measure epistemic uncertainty; it is an arbitrary stochastic perturbation. Calling the method Bayesian active learning is overstated.

Novelty is limited. Applying BALD-style disagreement or attention entropy to noise-seed selection is an incremental adaptation of existing active-learning and seed-selection ideas. The claim of being the first active noise-selection framework for video diffusion is narrow and does not constitute a major conceptual advance.

Evaluation is weak for a top-tier venue. Only CogVideoX-2B and CogVideoX-5B are tested, which are two scales of the same architecture, despite claims about 'various text-to-video architectures.' No official comparisons to FreeInit or FreqPrior are provided, and no external-metric or best-of-M oracle baselines are reported.

The reported gains are very small and lack statistical support: total VBench score improves by +0.63 on 2B and +0.25 on 5B, with quality improvements of +0.48 and +0.17. No confidence intervals, variance, or significance tests are given, so these differences may be within noise.

The method relies on several arbitrary design choices, including Bernoulli masking probability p=0.2, layer cutoff d*, noise pool size M, and ensemble size K, but only K and M are partially ablated. The layer-selection criterion is also described inconsistently as correlation with full-layer BANSA versus correlation with official quality scores.
Reproducibility is limited: no code link or project page is visible, prompts are promised only 'upon code release,' and key implementation details are underspecified.
There is no discussion of ethical concerns such as misuse for deepfakes, bias in generated videos, or computational/environmental impact, which is expected for generative video models.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated inference-time noise selection framework for video diffusion models, targeting the important problem that initial noise seeds strongly affect generation quality and prompt alignment.
Adapts BALD-style uncertainty estimation to attention maps, providing a principled acquisition function (BANSA) with an intuitive zero-disagreement condition and layer-wise interpretability.

Offers practical efficiency mechanisms: Bernoulli-masked attention approximates multiple attention samples in a single forward pass, and correlation-based layer truncation reduces cost while preserving ranking performance.
Demonstrates consistent improvements on CogVideoX-2B and CogVideoX-5B using VBench, with gains in semantic alignment and quality and a modest inference overhead (+8% and +13%).

Includes useful ablations on acquisition functions, ensemble size K, noise pool size M, reversed BANSA selection, and full-layer vs. truncated BANSA, which support the empirical effectiveness of the proposed components.
The paper is generally clear, well-illustrated, and acknowledges limitations, including failure cases and the gap between attention uncertainty and perceptual quality.
The method is orthogonal to external noise-prior approaches and could in principle be combined with them, which is a useful property for inference-time scaling.
weaknesses: The paper omits direct comparison with the most relevant prior noise initialization methods (FreeInit, FreqPrior, PYoCo), despite motivating the work against them and claiming lower cost with comparable or superior quality. This is a major evidentiary gap.

The reported gains are small: total VBench score improves by only +0.63 on CogVideoX-2B and +0.25 on CogVideoX-5B, with quality gains of +0.48 and +0.17. No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are provided, so the improvements may be within noise.

There is a sign-convention inconsistency between the main paper and appendix: the main text defines BANSA as mean entropy minus entropy of the mean, while the appendix implements the BALD-style entropy of the mean minus mean entropy. The paper claims equivalence of ordering, but the presentation is confusing and weakens theoretical clarity.

The Bernoulli-masked attention approximation is not a principled Bayesian posterior over model parameters; it measures sensitivity to random masking rather than true epistemic uncertainty. The connection between this perturbation-based attention disagreement and final video quality is largely empirical and not deeply justified.

The layer-selection criterion is inconsistently described: Section 3.3 says d* is chosen by correlation with the full-layer BANSA score, while Appendix E says it is chosen by correlation with official quality scores. If benchmark quality scores are used for hyperparameter selection, this raises potential benchmark tuning/leakage concerns.

Seed-selection baselines are weak: the paper compares only random, predictive entropy, and two BANSA variants. It lacks comparisons to simple prompt-alignment or quality-based selection strategies, or best-of-M selection using external metrics.

Evaluation is limited to CogVideoX-2B/5B. Despite claims of generalizability, no other T2V architectures (e.g., Open-Sora, Wan, HunyuanVideo) are tested, and the method is not evaluated on image diffusion or broader generative settings.

Hyperparameters such as Bernoulli probability p=0.2, correlation threshold tau=0.7, K=10, and M=10 appear tuned, but sensitivity analyses for p and tau are missing, reducing confidence in robustness and reproducibility.
No code or project-page artifacts appear to be available yet, and some implementation details are underspecified. Reproducibility is therefore only partially supported.

The method only selects the initial seed and does not change the generation process; the paper acknowledges that low-BANSA seeds can still produce unnatural videos. This limits the practical reliability of the approach and suggests the title's framing may be stronger than the evidence.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: initial noise seed selection strongly affects text-to-video diffusion outputs, and the paper proposes an inference-time selection framework without retraining.
Introduces BANSA, a BALD-style acquisition function adapted to attention maps, with a clean zero-condition proof via Jensen's inequality.
Provides an efficient approximation using Bernoulli-masked attention and truncated layer selection, making the method plug-and-play with modest reported overhead.
Evaluates on several T2V backbones (AnimateDiff, CogVideoX-2B/5B, Wan2.1, HunyuanVideo), includes ablations on acquisition function, K, M, masking probability, reversal, and a user study.
Shows compatibility with an existing frequency-prior method (FreqPrior) and reports FVMD motion metrics and qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: noise initialization/selection and uncertainty-based acquisition are existing ideas; the adaptation to attention maps via Bernoulli masking is not a fundamental advance for top-tier AI.

The theoretical grounding is weak: Bernoulli masking of post-softmax attention probabilities is not a justified Bayesian posterior over model parameters, so BANSA-E does not clearly estimate epistemic uncertainty as claimed.

Quantitative gains are marginal and inconsistent: e.g., CogVideoX-5B total score improves only from 81.52 to 81.71, HunyuanVideo aesthetic quality decreases, Wan2.1 aesthetic quality decreases, and several paper claims of consistent improvement are overstated.

Baselines are insufficient: FreqPrior is only evaluated on AnimateDiff; FreeInit/FreeNoise/PYoCo and other seed-selection or noise-initialization methods are not compared in the main tables; random/entropy baselines are only on CogVideoX-2B.
Semantic evaluation is omitted for HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, so prompt alignment for recent backbones is not actually assessed despite being a core claim.

There are numerous inconsistent/erroneous numbers across tables: Table 5 vs. Table 19 disagree on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 scores (e.g., aesthetic quality 0.6268 vs. 0.8268; background consistency 0.9656 vs. 0.9838), and several appendix confidence intervals are malformed (lower bound greater than mean or upper bound).
The statistical validation is not credible: reported 95% CIs overlap, contain impossible values, and are computed in a non-standard way; no proper significance tests support the claimed improvements.

The layer-selection procedure may be circular or overfit: d* is chosen by correlation with the full-layer BANSA score, which itself is not independently validated as a quality predictor, and uses the same 100 prompts/seeds across models without held-out validation.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is specified, the project page link is blank, the full prompt list is only promised upon release, and key implementation details (e.g., masking of all-zero rows, exact layer choices) are incomplete.

Clarity and writing quality are poor: many typos and grammatical errors ('jigful', 'flang', 'signicanse', 'HunyuanVideo' vs. 'HunyangVideo', 'AnimateDiff' spacing, 'IPOC' vs. 'IPoC'), which hampers evaluation.

Practical significance is questionable: the method adds roughly 8–15% inference overhead for small VBench gains, and it is unclear whether it outperforms simply sampling/selecting more seeds under the same compute budget.
User study reporting is thin: only 12 evaluators and 30 prompts, with no inter-annotator agreement or statistical analysis, so human preference evidence is weak.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: initial noise seeds strongly affect text-to-video generation quality and consistency.
Proposes a model-aware, training-free inference-time selection method instead of relying only on external frequency priors.
Introduces an efficient Bernoulli-masked approximation and layer truncation to reduce the cost of uncertainty estimation.
Evaluates on multiple T2V backbones (AnimateDiff, CogVideoX-2B/5B, HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1) with VBench, FVMD, ablations, and a user study.
Reports lower overhead than full diffusion-based noise refinement baselines such as FreqPrior and shows compatibility with FreqPrior.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: BANSA is essentially a BALD-style entropy-disagreement score applied to attention maps for seed ranking; the 'Bayesian active noise selection' framing is not convincingly justified.

Theoretical grounding is weak: Bernoulli masking of attention maps is an arbitrary perturbation, not a posterior sample over model parameters, so BANSA does not clearly estimate epistemic uncertainty in a Bayesian sense.

The central assumption that lower attention uncertainty implies higher video quality is not rigorously established; correlations are only moderate (~0.67), and the paper admits low-BANSA seeds can still produce unnatural videos.
The Bernoulli-masked approximation and layer-selection procedure lack sufficient justification and may be sensitive to architecture, masking probability p, and selected layer depth d*.
Evaluation gains are very small: e.g., CogVideoX-5B total score improves from 81.52 to 81.71, and several HunyuanVideo/Wan2.1 gains are marginal and likely within noise.
Important baselines are missing: FreeInit and other noise-selection/optimization methods are not compared on most backbones, and no strong alternative inference-time scaling baseline is provided.

Several reported tables appear inconsistent or erroneous: HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 vanilla metrics are identical in Table 5; aesthetic scores differ sharply between Table 5 and Table 19; some confidence intervals in Tables 17 and 18 are invalid or do not contain the reported mean.

The layer-selection protocol is unclear: the main text describes correlating partial and full-layer BANSA, while Appendix D describes correlating BANSA with official quality scores, raising concerns about tuning and possible test-data leakage.

Computational overhead of +8-15% is not obviously marginal for large video diffusion models; the paper also does not fully account for the cost of evaluating M seeds with K stochastic attention samples.
The user study lacks sufficient detail: no raw preference counts, statistical significance tests, inter-rater agreement, or evaluator background information are provided.
Reproducibility is concerning: no code or project page link is given, model-specific d* and prompt sets are not released, and the method requires tuning of p, K, M, and layer depth.
Qualitative results appear selected, and the failure case shows the method does not overcome fundamental model limitations or ensure high-quality outputs.
The term 'active' is used loosely: the method does not perform active learning or data acquisition but simply ranks a fixed pool of initial noise seeds at inference time.
The paper does not discuss ethical or misuse considerations for generated video content.

strengths: Proposes a novel inference-time noise seed selection framework for video diffusion, using model-internal attention uncertainty rather than external noise priors.
Introduces BANSA, a BALD-style acquisition function adapted to attention maps, with Bernoulli-masked attention for efficient single-pass stochastic sampling and correlation-based layer truncation.
Evaluates across several T2V backbones (AnimateDiff, CogVideoX-2B/5B, Wan2.1, HunyuanVideo) and includes many ablations (K, M, Bernoulli p, reversed BANSA, CFG, temporal scope, attention type).
Reports some consistent improvements on VBench quality/semantic scores, FVMD motion metrics, and a small user preference study.
Discusses limitations, including that low-BANSA seeds can still produce unnatural content and that the method does not modify the sampling process.
weaknesses: The theoretical grounding is weak: BANSA is not a genuine Bayesian/BALD uncertainty estimate over model parameters. Attention maps are not predictive distributions, and Bernoulli masking injects artificial stochasticity, so the score may primarily measure sensitivity to masking rather than epistemic uncertainty.
The Bayesian/active-learning framing is overstated: no posterior over parameters is used, and the zero-condition proposition is a trivial consequence of Jensen's inequality.

Evaluation contains serious inconsistencies. In Table 5, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 vanilla rows are nearly identical across most metrics, as are their +Ours rows, which is highly suspicious for two different backbones. Main-text Table 5 and Appendix Table 19 also disagree sharply on HunyuanVideo Aesthetic Quality (0.6268 vs 0.8268). Appendix CI tables contain invalid intervals (e.g., lower bound greater than mean/upper bound) and garbled metric names.

Reported gains are often very small and not consistently positive: e.g., CogVideoX-5B total score improves only 0.19, and several metrics degrade, such as Aesthetic Quality in Tables 5 and 11, Imaging Quality for Wan2.1 14B, and Background Consistency for IPOC-2B. Statistical significance is not convincingly established.

Baseline comparisons are insufficient: FreeInit is discussed but not quantitatively compared in the main tables, FreqPrior is only compared on AnimateDiff, and there is no comparison to simple seed-selection heuristics (e.g., low-frequency heuristics, random selection from the same noise pool, or oracle best-of-M). This makes it unclear whether gains come from BANSA or merely from evaluating multiple seeds.

The efficiency claim is weak: the method adds roughly 10–15% inference overhead for marginal quality gains, and the overhead may be larger in less optimized implementations. Calling this 'marginal' is not well justified for all backbones.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or project URL is provided, the layer-selection threshold 0.7 and d* choices are heuristic, and important implementation details (e.g., renormalization under Bernoulli masking, handling empty rows, exact attention layers used) are incomplete.

Novelty is incremental: the core idea is an adaptation of BALD/active learning to attention maps for seed selection, combined with known masking and layer-truncation tricks. The claim of being the 'first active noise selection framework' is not convincingly substantiated against prior noise optimization and initialization work.
The user study is small (12 evaluators, 30 prompts) and lacks inter-annotator agreement or confidence intervals, limiting its evidential value.
